html:
The Hedypatheia, "Life of Luxury", is a comic poem about food written in the mid 4th century BCE by Archestratus of Gela, a Greek city in Sicily. It is one of the oldest cookery guides in Europe.

Archestratus wrote in the grand verse of epic, the metre of Homer, but his subject was where to find the best things to eat around the Greek world. He travelled widely and named the best place to buy each fish: tuna at Byzantium, for example. He liked simple cooking that let good fish speak for itself, with a little oil and salt, and he mocked cooks who drowned it in cheese and heavy sauces.

The poem itself is lost. About sixty fragments survive because Athenaeus, a writer of about 200 CE, quoted them in his huge book of dinner table talk. The Roman poet Ennius made a Latin version. The poem shows a Greek world joined by trade in food and wine, the world of the symposium and of the olive oil and wine trade.
